cloze.sentence: Our team takes a ___ approach and prevents delays before they happen.

formDrill.sentence: The nurses ___ checked every patient before the storm.

fix.wrong: He is very proactive to solve problems.
fix.right: He is very proactive in solving problems.
fix.why: Use "proactive in" + -ing.

distractors: Reacting only after trouble has happened.
Very active and always busy.
Careful not to spend too much money.
tip: The opposite is "reactive".

definition: Having a certain value, or good enough to deserve your time or effort.
examples: This car is worth about five million naira.
The film is worth watching if you like thrillers.

pattern.example: The book is worth reading twice.

cloze.sentence: Is it ___ paying more for a faster internet plan?

formDrill.sentence: A ___ cause deserves our support.

fix.wrong: It is worth to visit the museum.
fix.right: It is worth visiting the museum.
fix.why: "Worth" is followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: Costing much less than expected.
Very important to a small group of people.
Easy to find in any shop.
tip: Say "worth doing", never "worth to do".

definition: To use something you already have in a way that gives you the most benefit.
examples: She leveraged her network to find a new job.
We can leverage social media to reach more customers.

pattern.example: The company leveraged its brand to launch a new product.

cloze.sentence: Small businesses can ___ free online tools to save money.

formDrill.sentence: By ___ his experience, he negotiated a better salary.

fix.wrong: We leverage on our contacts.
fix.right: We leverage our contacts.
fix.why: "Leverage" is transitive; do not add "on".

distractors: To lift a heavy object using a bar.
To borrow money without paying it back.
To waste a resource through poor planning.
tip: Common in business English; in everyday speech, "use" is often simpler.

definition: Careful and slightly afraid because you think something may be dangerous or dishonest.
examples: Be wary of emails asking for your password.
The farmers were wary of the new loan scheme.

pattern.example: I am wary of sharing my phone number.

cloze.sentence: After being cheated once, he is ___ of strangers who offer deals.

formDrill.sentence: She ___ checked the stairs before stepping onto them.

fix.wrong: I am wary about the strangers.
fix.right: I am wary of strangers.
fix.why: "Wary" normally takes "of".

distractors: Very tired after a long day.
Happy to try something new.
Ready to forgive someone quickly.
tip: Wary is milder than "afraid" and is not the same as "weary" (tired).

definition: Showing a clear and deep understanding of a person or situation.
examples: Her insightful comments helped us see the real problem.
It was an insightful article about why young people change jobs.

pattern.example: He gave an insightful talk about customer habits.

cloze.sentence: The consultant offered an ___ report on why sales fell.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ into customer needs helped the team improve the app.

fix.wrong: Thank you for your insight comment.
fix.right: Thank you for your insightful comment.
fix.why: The adjective is "insightful"; "insight" is the noun.

distractors: Quick to criticize other people.
Not interested in learning details.
Easy to understand without effort.

definition: To say that something is not true, or to refuse to give or allow something.
examples: He denied taking the money from the till.
The bank denied her request for a loan.

pattern.example: She denied breaking the window.

cloze.sentence: The minister ___ the rumor and called it false.

formDrill.sentence: After the accident, the driver was in ___ and refused to talk.

fix.wrong: He denied to have stolen the phone.
fix.right: He denied stealing the phone.
fix.why: "Deny" is followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To admit something after a long delay.
To promise to do something soon.
To forget an important fact.
tip: Deny + -ing: "She denied taking it." Do not say "deny to do".

definition: Making you feel nervous or less confident because something seems very difficult.
examples: Moving to a new country alone is a daunting prospect.
The pile of unpaid bills looked daunting.

pattern.rule: daunting + noun / it is daunting + to + verb
pattern.example: It is daunting to speak in front of five hundred people.

cloze.sentence: Starting a business with no savings is a ___ challenge.

formDrill.sentence: Do not let the long list ___ you; take one task at a time.

fix.wrong: I felt very daunting before the exam.
fix.right: I felt daunted before the exam.
fix.why: "Daunting" describes the task; "daunted" describes how you feel.

distractors: Boring and repeating the same steps.
Easy to finish before lunch.
Unfair to some of the people involved.
tip: Daunting describes the task; "daunted" describes the person.

definition: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings.
examples: A good nurse shows empathy for frightened patients.
Managers need empathy to understand why staff are stressed.

pattern.example: She has great empathy for her students.

cloze.sentence: Listening without judging is a sign of ___.

formDrill.sentence: It is hard to ___ with someone whose life is so different from yours.

fix.wrong: He has no empathy to other people.
fix.right: He has no empathy for other people.
fix.why: Use "empathy for" or "empathy with".

distractors: A strong wish to help people for money.
The feeling of being sorry for yourself.
Very strong anger towards someone.
tip: Empathy is feeling WITH someone; sympathy is feeling sorry FOR them.

definition: A difficult situation in which you must choose between two options, neither of which is good.
examples: She faced a dilemma: take the higher salary or stay near her family.
The manager was in a dilemma about whom to promote.

pattern.rule: dilemma + about / over + noun; in a dilemma
pattern.example: He is in a dilemma about which job to accept.

cloze.sentence: I am in a ___: I want to help my friend, but it means missing work.

formDrill.sentence: Doctors often face ethical ___ at work.

fix.wrong: I have a big dilemma to choose a school.
fix.right: I have a big dilemma about choosing a school.
fix.why: Use "dilemma about/over" and not a to-infinitive.

distractors: A small mistake that is easy to correct.
A problem with only one clear answer.
An argument between two close friends.
tip: A dilemma has two hard choices; do not use it for any small problem.

definition: To give someone support or hope so that they do something, or to make something more likely.
examples: Her parents encouraged her to apply for the scholarship.
The new bonus scheme encourages workers to arrive early.

pattern.example: The teacher encouraged us to ask questions.

cloze.sentence: Managers should ___ staff to share their ideas.

formDrill.sentence: Thank you for your constant ___ during my studies.

fix.wrong: He encouraged me applying for the job.
fix.right: He encouraged me to apply for the job.
fix.why: Encourage + person + to + verb, not -ing.

distractors: To order someone to do a task.
To warn someone about a danger.
To make someone feel ashamed.
tip: Encourage someone TO do something; the opposite is "discourage someone FROM doing".

definition: Something that makes people want to do something, such as a reward or a benefit.
examples: The company offers an incentive of free lunch for early arrival.
Lower taxes are an incentive for people to start businesses.

pattern.example: There is little incentive to save when prices rise so fast.

cloze.sentence: The discount is an ___ for customers to pay early.

formDrill.sentence: Companies often ___ staff with extra pay for good results.

fix.wrong: He has no incentive for working harder.
fix.right: He has no incentive to work harder.
fix.why: "Incentive" is followed by "to" + verb.

distractors: A rule that people must obey.
A punishment for breaking a rule.
A report about a problem at work.
tip: Incentive is a reward that encourages action; a "bonus" is one kind of incentive.

definition: Giving all the necessary information in few words.
examples: Please write a concise summary of the meeting.
Her email was short and concise.

pattern.example: Keep your message concise.

cloze.sentence: Managers prefer ___ reports that get to the point quickly.

formDrill.sentence: She explained the rules ___ in two sentences.

fix.wrong: Please be concise on your answer.
fix.right: Please be concise in your answer.
fix.why: Use "in your answer" with "concise".

distractors: Long and full of small details.
Written in a very formal style.
Easy to read aloud to others.
tip: Concise means short but complete; "brief" can mean short but missing detail.

definition: Not very good; of only average or disappointing quality.
examples: The food was mediocre and the service was slow.
He gave a mediocre performance in the interview.

pattern.example: The hotel was mediocre for the price.

cloze.sentence: I expected a great film, but it was ___ at best.

formDrill.sentence: He refused to accept ___ and kept improving his work.

fix.wrong: The food was mediocrity.
fix.right: The food was mediocre.
fix.why: After 'was', use the adjective 'mediocre', not the noun.

distractors: Excellent and better than most.
Very bad and unacceptable.
Expensive and full of detail.
tip: Mediocre is negative: it is worse than "average" because it suggests disappointment.

definition: To think carefully about something before making a decision.
examples: We are considering moving to a bigger flat.
Please consider my offer before you answer.

pattern.example: I am considering changing my job.

cloze.sentence: I will ___ your request and give you an answer tomorrow.

formDrill.sentence: It was very ___ of you to call and check on me.

fix.wrong: I am considering to buy a car.
fix.right: I am considering buying a car.
fix.why: "Consider" is followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To forget something on purpose.
To ask someone a direct question.
To agree with someone immediately.
tip: Consider + -ing: "I considered leaving". Do not say "consider to leave".

definition: Done without any plan or order, so that the result is careless or random.
examples: The files were stored in a haphazard way, so nothing was easy to find.
Their haphazard planning caused the event to fail.

pattern.rule: haphazard + noun / in a haphazard way
pattern.example: The books were piled in a haphazard way.

cloze.sentence: Boxes were stacked in a ___ way, and one fell on his foot.

formDrill.sentence: The papers were thrown ___ on the desk.

fix.wrong: The room was arranged haphazard.
fix.right: The room was arranged haphazardly.
fix.why: Use the adverb "haphazardly" after a verb.

distractors: Planned in great detail.
Done quickly and neatly.
Done only when someone is watching.

definition: Not certain or final; offered carefully because you are unsure.
examples: We made a tentative plan to meet on Friday.
She gave a tentative smile before speaking.

pattern.example: They reached a tentative agreement on the price.

cloze.sentence: The date for the launch is only ___; it may change.

formDrill.sentence: He ___ suggested a new idea, unsure how the team would react.

fix.wrong: Our plan is still tentatively.
fix.right: Our plan is still tentative.
fix.why: "Tentative" is the adjective; "tentatively" modifies a verb.

distractors: Fixed and impossible to change.
Strongly opposed to something.
Very confident and bold.

definition: Only on the surface; not deep or thorough.
examples: The cut was superficial and healed in a few days.
His knowledge of the subject is superficial.

pattern.example: The report gave only a superficial analysis.

cloze.sentence: A ___ look at the data will not show the real problem.

formDrill.sentence: The two phones are ___ similar, but they work very differently.

fix.wrong: He gave a superficially answer.
fix.right: He gave a superficial answer.
fix.why: Use the adjective "superficial" before a noun.

distractors: Very deep and based on long study.
Related to the top part of a building.
Very friendly and open to others.
tip: It can describe a person who cares only about appearance: "a superficial person".

definition: To make someone agree to do or believe something by giving good reasons.
examples: I persuaded my brother to lend me his laptop.
She was persuaded by the clear evidence in the report.

pattern.rule: persuade + object + to + verb / that + clause
pattern.example: He persuaded her to stay longer.

cloze.sentence: Nothing can ___ me to sign that contract.

formDrill.sentence: She made a ___ argument, and the board agreed.

fix.wrong: I persuaded him for join us.
fix.right: I persuaded him to join us.
fix.why: "Persuade" takes object + to-infinitive.

distractors: To force someone by using threats.
To ask someone a difficult question.
To feel sure about something yourself.

definition: A warm, slightly sad feeling when you think about happy times in the past.
examples: Hearing that old song filled him with nostalgia.
There is a lot of nostalgia for 1990s music.

pattern.example: She felt nostalgia for her school days.

cloze.sentence: Looking at old photos brought back a wave of ___.

formDrill.sentence: He felt ___ when he returned to his childhood home.

fix.wrong: I have nostalgia of my village.
fix.right: I have nostalgia for my village.
fix.why: Use "nostalgia for".

distractors: A strong fear of going outside.
A feeling of anger about the past.
A plan for a future event.
tip: Say "nostalgic for" or "nostalgia for"; you may also feel nostalgic about something.

definition: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other well.
examples: A good teacher builds rapport with students quickly.
There was an easy rapport between the two colleagues.

pattern.example: She has a good rapport with her clients.

cloze.sentence: It takes time to build ___ with a new team.

fix.wrong: He has a good rapport to his boss.
fix.right: He has a good rapport with his boss.
fix.why: Use "rapport with" or "rapport between".

distractors: A written report about a meeting.
A strong argument between two people.
A formal rule about how to behave.
tip: The final "t" is silent: say "ra-POR". Not the same as "report".

definition: To say something again, usually to make a point clear or strong.
examples: I want to reiterate that the deadline will not change.
The manager reiterated his support for the plan.

pattern.example: Let me reiterate our main goal.

cloze.sentence: At the end of the talk, she ___ the key message.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ of the rules did not change anything.

fix.wrong: I want to reiterate again that we start Monday.
fix.right: I want to reiterate that we start Monday.
fix.why: "Reiterate" already means "say again", so "again" is redundant.

distractors: To change a statement completely.
To ask a question more than once.
To cancel a decision made earlier.
tip: Formal. In everyday speech, say "repeat" or "say again".

definition: Correct and exact, with no mistakes.
examples: The report must be accurate before we send it to the client.
His weather forecast was accurate all week.

pattern.example: Is this information accurate?

cloze.sentence: Please check that the figures in the invoice are ___.

formDrill.sentence: She described the accident ___ to the police.

fix.wrong: The news was not accuracy.
fix.right: The news was not accurate.
fix.why: Use the adjective "accurate" after "was".

distractors: Quick to be completed.
Very surprising to most people.
Based on opinion, not on facts.
tip: Accurate means correct; "precise" means exact in small detail. Something can be precise but not accurate.

definition: To feel true or meaningful to someone; also, to make a deep, echoing sound.
examples: Her story about starting over really resonated with the audience.
The sound of the drums resonated through the hall.

pattern.example: The speech resonated with young voters.

cloze.sentence: If an advert does not ___ with people, they will ignore it.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of his words stayed with me for days.

fix.wrong: Her message resonated to me.
fix.right: Her message resonated with me.
fix.why: Use "resonate with" for the person who feels it.

distractors: To make someone feel confused.
To disagree strongly with someone.
To repeat words from memory.

definition: To make two different ideas agree, or to make people friends again after a fight.
examples: It is hard to reconcile a full-time job with studying.
The two brothers reconciled after years of silence.

pattern.rule: reconcile + A + with + B; reconcile with + person
pattern.example: She tried to reconcile her beliefs with her work.

cloze.sentence: The accountant had to ___ the bank statement with the company records.

formDrill.sentence: After the argument, there was a quick ___ between the friends.

fix.wrong: It is difficult to reconcile work to family.
fix.right: It is difficult to reconcile work with family.
fix.why: Use 'reconcile A with B'.

distractors: To divide something into equal parts.
To forget a past disagreement completely.
To compare two prices before buying.
tip: In accounting, to "reconcile" means to check that two sets of records match.

definition: To join several smaller things into one bigger, stronger or simpler whole.
examples: The bank plans to consolidate its three branches in Ikeja into one office.
I consolidated all my small loans into a single monthly payment.

pattern.example: She consolidated the files into one folder.

cloze.sentence: After years of growth, the company needs to ___ its position in the market.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of the two schools saved the district a lot of money.

fix.wrong: We consolidate together all our reports.
fix.right: We consolidate all our reports.
fix.why: Consolidate already means to bring together, so do not add "together".

distractors: To make something simpler by removing parts of it.
To divide a large group into separate smaller ones.
To check something carefully for mistakes.
tip: Consolidate also means to make a position or success stronger, e.g. "consolidate a lead".

definition: Working well and quickly without wasting time, money or energy.
examples: Our new software makes the payroll process much more efficient.
A small fridge can be efficient if you shop for a few days at a time.

pattern.example: He is efficient at handling customer complaints.

cloze.sentence: The new generator is far more ___ and uses half the fuel.

formDrill.sentence: She finished the whole report ___ in under an hour.

fix.wrong: She is very efficient on managing her time.
fix.right: She is very efficient at managing her time.
fix.why: Use "efficient at" + -ing.

distractors: Very friendly and polite to everyone you meet.
Able to produce something unusually creative.
Cheap and easy to buy in large amounts.
tip: Efficient is about how well something is done; effective is about whether it achieves the result.

definition: Very careful and paying close attention to every small detail.
examples: She keeps meticulous records of every payment she makes.
The report was meticulous; not a single number was wrong.

pattern.example: He is meticulous about checking his work.

cloze.sentence: Our accountant is ___; she checks every receipt twice.

formDrill.sentence: The wedding was ___ planned, down to the seating cards.

fix.wrong: He is meticulous of his appearance.
fix.right: He is meticulous about his appearance.
fix.why: Use "meticulous about", not "of".

distractors: Easily upset by small problems.
Quick and careless in finishing tasks.
Very generous with time and money.
tip: Meticulous is a compliment; for excessive carefulness, say "fussy" or "pedantic".

definition: To make something bad, such as a risk or a harm, less serious.
examples: Planting trees along the road helps mitigate the effects of flooding.
We mitigated the risk by backing up all our files every night.

pattern.example: Insurance can mitigate the cost of an accident.

cloze.sentence: The company hired extra staff to ___ the impact of the strike.

formDrill.sentence: Climate ___ projects aim to reduce harm to coastal towns.

fix.wrong: They want to mitigate against the risk of fraud.
fix.right: They want to mitigate the risk of fraud.
fix.why: Mitigate is transitive and takes no preposition; "militate against" is a different verb.

distractors: To make a problem more serious on purpose.
To officially announce a coming change.
To settle an argument between two people.
tip: Do not confuse mitigate (reduce harm) with militate (act against).

definition: A small, subtle difference in meaning, tone or feeling.
examples: There is a nuance between "I can't" and "I won't" that learners often miss.
The translation lost some of the nuance of the original speech.

pattern.rule: nuance of + noun; countable (a nuance, nuances)
pattern.example: She understands the nuances of office politics.

cloze.sentence: A good translator must capture every ___ of the original text.

formDrill.sentence: It was a thoughtful and ___ discussion with no simple answers.

fix.wrong: There are many nuance in this word.
fix.right: There are many nuances in this word.
fix.why: Nuance is countable; use the plural nuances.

distractors: A very strong feeling of worry about the future.
A clear and direct instruction from a manager.
A large difference between two prices.
tip: Nuance is countable; people often say "the nuances of" a language, culture or situation.

definition: Having the duty to deal with something, or deserving blame or credit for it.
examples: Who is responsible for ordering supplies for the office?
Parents are responsible for making sure their children get to school safely.

pattern.example: He is responsible for training new staff.

cloze.sentence: The driver was ___ for the accident because he ignored the red light.

formDrill.sentence: Please drink ___ and never drive after a party.

fix.wrong: She is responsible of the sales team.
fix.right: She is responsible for the sales team.
fix.why: Use "responsible for", not "of".

distractors: Willing to spend money without thinking.
Able to answer quickly in a difficult situation.
Friendly and polite to customers.
tip: You are responsible to a person (your boss) but responsible for a task or result.

definition: Able to express ideas clearly and effectively in speech or writing.
examples: She is an articulate speaker who explains complex issues simply.
The young candidate was confident and articulate in the interview.

pattern.rule: articulate (adj) vs articulate (verb: to express clearly)
pattern.example: He articulated his concerns calmly at the meeting.

cloze.sentence: A good lawyer must be ___ and able to persuade a jury.

formDrill.sentence: He ___ his vision for the company clearly in the first meeting.

fix.wrong: He articulated very good in the interview.
fix.right: He was very articulate in the interview.
fix.why: Articulate is an adjective here; "articulated" is a verb that needs an object.

distractors: Hard to understand because of mumbling.
Very quiet and unwilling to speak up.
Able to speak many different languages.
tip: The verb is pronounced /ɑːrˈtɪk.jə.leɪt/ and the adjective /ɑːrˈtɪk.jə.lət/.

definition: Able to speak or write in a fluent, persuasive and powerful way.
examples: The pastor gave an eloquent speech that moved the whole congregation.
Her eloquent letter convinced the board to reconsider.

pattern.example: She was eloquent about the need for better schools.

cloze.sentence: His ___ plea for peace made many people in the hall cry.

formDrill.sentence: She spoke ___ about her late father at the funeral.

fix.wrong: He is very eloquent in speaking English fast.
fix.right: He is very eloquent when he speaks.
fix.why: Eloquent means persuasive and well expressed, not just fast.

distractors: Speaking in a loud, angry voice.
Speaking only a few words at a time.
Able to remember long speeches word for word.
tip: Eloquent is stronger than "fluent": it suggests beauty and persuasive power.

definition: Very deep or strong, affecting you in an important way.
examples: The news of his death had a profound effect on the whole team.
She felt a profound sense of relief when the results came out.

pattern.rule: profound + effect / impact / change / sense of
pattern.example: The move to Canada had a profound influence on her.

cloze.sentence: The new law will have a ___ impact on small businesses.

formDrill.sentence: He was ___ disappointed by the decision.

fix.wrong: The book gave me a profound impression about life.
fix.right: The book gave me a profound impression of life.
fix.why: Say "an impression of" something.

distractors: Shallow and quickly forgotten.
Slightly annoying but not important.
Easy to understand without effort.
tip: Profound is usually used with big ideas, feelings and changes, not everyday objects.

definition: Willing to give more money, time or help than is expected.
examples: My uncle is generous and always pays for the family's school fees.
The company offered a generous severance package.

pattern.rule: generous + with + noun / generous + of + person + to-infinitive
pattern.example: It was generous of her to lend us the car.

cloze.sentence: The restaurant serves ___ portions, so we always take leftovers home.

formDrill.sentence: She gave ___ to the charity every December.

fix.wrong: He is very generous of his time.
fix.right: He is very generous with his time.
fix.why: Use 'generous with' something you give.

distractors: Careful to spend money only on needs.
Proud of your own achievements.
Quick to forgive other people.
tip: You can also use generous for amounts: "a generous helping" means a large one.

definition: To examine something very closely and carefully, often looking for mistakes.
examples: The auditors scrutinized every invoice from last year.
Customs officers scrutinize the passports of all arriving passengers.

pattern.rule: scrutinize + noun; scrutiny is the noun (under scrutiny)
pattern.example: The committee will scrutinize the budget.

cloze.sentence: Before signing, always ___ the small print of a loan agreement.

formDrill.sentence: The minister's spending came under public ___.

fix.wrong: The teacher scrutinized at my essay.
fix.right: The teacher scrutinized my essay.
fix.why: Scrutinize is transitive and takes no preposition.

distractors: To admire something from far away.
To change something to make it look better.
To approve something without reading it.
tip: The British spelling is scrutinise.

definition: To limit or restrict what someone or something can do.
examples: A small budget constrains what we can offer our customers.
Poor roads constrained the growth of local trade.

pattern.example: The team was constrained by a tight deadline.

cloze.sentence: Limited funding will ___ how many students the school can accept.

formDrill.sentence: The project faced several time ___ and had to cut features.

fix.wrong: The budget is constrained from the lack of funds.
fix.right: The budget is constrained by a lack of funds.
fix.why: Use "constrained by" to show the cause.

distractors: To pull something tightly together.
To make something bigger and more powerful.
To give someone full freedom to act.
tip: Constrain often appears in the passive: "We are constrained by time."

definition: To think deeply about something for a long time, or to consider doing it.
examples: She is contemplating a career change after ten years in banking.
He sat by the window and contemplated his next move.

pattern.example: They are contemplating moving to Abuja.

cloze.sentence: I never ___ leaving this job until the offer came.

formDrill.sentence: He sat in quiet ___ for a few minutes before replying.

fix.wrong: She is contemplating to open a shop.
fix.right: She is contemplating opening a shop.
fix.why: Contemplate is followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To refuse to accept something.
To look at something very briefly.
To discuss a plan loudly with others.
tip: Contemplate is more serious and formal than "think about".

definition: Feeling worried or nervous, especially about something that may happen.
examples: I felt anxious while waiting for my visa interview.
Her parents were anxious about her traveling alone at night.

pattern.rule: anxious + about + noun / -ing; anxious + to + verb (eager)
pattern.example: He is anxious about the exam results.

cloze.sentence: The whole family waited ___ for news from the hospital.

formDrill.sentence: She suffers from ___ before every big presentation.

fix.wrong: I am anxious for my interview tomorrow.
fix.right: I am anxious about my interview tomorrow.
fix.why: Use "anxious about" for worry; "anxious for" means wanting something.

distractors: Calm and relaxed about the future.
Extremely angry about something unfair.
Very excited and happy about good news.
tip: "Anxious to do something" means eager to do it, as in "anxious to get started".

definition: Following what is traditional or most common; not unusual or new.
examples: They had a conventional wedding in church followed by a party.
Solar power is cheaper than conventional electricity in some areas.

pattern.example: She took a conventional route into law.

cloze.sentence: Many farmers are moving away from ___ methods to organic ones.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ approach to teaching surprised the older staff.

fix.wrong: Is Monday conventional for you?
fix.right: Is Monday convenient for you?
fix.why: 'Conventional' means traditional; 'convenient' means suitable or easy.

distractors: Very modern and different from the norm.
Easy to change when needed.
Official and approved by the government.
tip: Conventional can sound slightly negative, meaning "ordinary" or "unimaginative".

definition: To show or describe someone or something in a picture, story or film.
examples: The film depicts life in Lagos in the 1970s.
The poster depicted a farmer holding a bag of rice.

pattern.example: The article depicts him as a hard-working leader.

cloze.sentence: The mural ___ scenes from the town's history.

formDrill.sentence: The report gave a bleak ___ of life in the camp.

fix.wrong: The book depicts about village life.
fix.right: The book depicts village life.
fix.why: Depict is transitive and takes no preposition after it.

distractors: To hide the truth from the public.
To make a copy of an original document.
To criticize something in a public speech.
tip: Depict is used for pictures, films, writing and stories, not for simply "saying" something.

definition: To notice or understand something that is not obvious, by looking or thinking carefully.
examples: It was hard to discern the road through the heavy rain.
I could discern a note of worry in her voice.

pattern.rule: discern + noun / that-clause / discern between A and B
pattern.example: Can you discern any difference between the two samples?

cloze.sentence: From the data, we can ___ a clear trend in customer behavior.

formDrill.sentence: Her ___ eye for talent helped her build a great team.

fix.wrong: I cannot discern the difference with these two.
fix.right: I cannot discern the difference between these two.
fix.why: Use "between" with two things.

distractors: To ignore a sign on purpose.
To argue strongly against an idea.
To carry out an order without question.
tip: Discern is formal; in everyday speech, use "notice" or "tell the difference".

definition: Not often; only a few times.
examples: He rarely checks his email on weekends.
We rarely eat out because it is so expensive.

pattern.rule: rarely goes before the main verb; already negative, so no "not"
pattern.example: She rarely arrives late.

cloze.sentence: I ___ see my cousins because they live abroad.

formDrill.sentence: Gold is a ___ metal found in only a few places.

fix.wrong: I don't rarely go to the gym.
fix.right: I rarely go to the gym.
fix.why: Rarely is already negative, so do not add "don't".

distractors: Very often and without fail.
Only at a particular time of year.
Always at the very last minute.
tip: After "rarely" at the start of a sentence, invert the verb: "Rarely have I seen such a mess."

definition: To try very hard to do something.
examples: We endeavor to reply to all emails within 24 hours.
She endeavored to finish the project before the deadline.

pattern.rule: endeavor + to + verb (formal); also a noun: a worthwhile endeavor
pattern.example: The school endeavors to support every student.

cloze.sentence: The airline will ___ to get your luggage back within two days.

formDrill.sentence: She ___ to reply to every email within a day.

fix.wrong: They endeavored for finishing the road on time.
fix.right: They endeavored to finish the road on time.
fix.why: Endeavor is followed by a to-infinitive.

distractors: To refuse to take part in something.
To plan something in secret.
To finish a job much earlier than expected.
tip: Endeavor is formal; "try" is more common in everyday speech. UK spelling is endeavour.

definition: An idea put forward as an explanation, which still needs to be tested.
examples: Our hypothesis is that customers prefer shorter delivery times.
The experiment failed to support the scientist's hypothesis.

pattern.example: Their hypothesis that sleep improves memory was confirmed.

cloze.sentence: The scientists spent a year trying to prove their ___ was correct.

formDrill.sentence: She asked a ___ question about what she would do if she won the lottery.

fix.wrong: The hypothesises were all proved wrong.
fix.right: The hypotheses were all proved wrong.
fix.why: The plural of hypothesis is hypotheses.

distractors: A fact that everyone already agrees on.
A final result that cannot be questioned.
A detailed plan for a new project.
tip: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation to be tested; a theory is usually already well supported.

definition: About to happen very soon, often something unpleasant.
examples: Forecasters warned that a storm was imminent.
The company is facing imminent collapse without new funding.

pattern.rule: be imminent (adjective only, not for people)
pattern.example: A decision is imminent.

cloze.sentence: Residents were told to leave because a flood was ___.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of the deadline made everyone nervous.

fix.wrong: Her arrival is imminent to happen.
fix.right: Her arrival is imminent.
fix.why: Imminent does not take "to happen"; it already means about to happen.

distractors: Very important and likely to last long.
Possible but not likely to happen.
Having already happened a long time ago.
tip: Do not confuse imminent (about to happen) with eminent (famous and respected).

definition: To agree that something is true, usually when you did not want to.
examples: He admitted that he had forgotten the meeting.
She admitted taking the money but promised to pay it back.

pattern.rule: admit + -ing / that-clause (not to-infinitive); admit to + noun
pattern.example: He admitted breaking the window.

cloze.sentence: I have to ___ that I did not read the whole contract.

formDrill.sentence: His ___ of guilt surprised the court.

fix.wrong: She admitted to make a mistake.
fix.right: She admitted making a mistake.
fix.why: After admit, use -ing or a that-clause, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To refuse to take responsibility for something.
To explain something in careful detail.
To forget something important.
tip: Admit also means to allow someone to enter, e.g. "admitted to hospital".

definition: Fair and not supporting one side more than another.
examples: A judge must be impartial and listen to both sides.
We need an impartial person to settle the dispute.

pattern.rule: impartial + noun; be impartial in / about
pattern.example: The referee stayed impartial throughout the match.

cloze.sentence: The inquiry was led by an ___ expert with no ties to either company.

formDrill.sentence: The judge must show ___ to everyone in the courtroom.

fix.wrong: A judge must be unpartial.
fix.right: A judge must be impartial.
fix.why: The opposite of 'partial' here is 'impartial', not 'unpartial'.

distractors: Strongly in favor of one side.
Quick to decide without thinking.
Not able to hear or listen well.
tip: Impartial is slightly more formal than "fair" and is common in law and news.

definition: Existing in something as a natural, permanent part of it.
examples: There are inherent risks in any new business.
Patience is inherent in the work of a teacher.

pattern.example: Some danger is inherent in mining.

cloze.sentence: Every investment has an ___ risk of losing money.

formDrill.sentence: Deep-sea fishing is ___ dangerous.

fix.wrong: The problem is inherent of the system.
fix.right: The problem is inherent in the system.
fix.why: Use "inherent in", not "of".

distractors: Received from a relative after their death.
Added to something later on.
Easy to see at once.
tip: Inherent (belonging naturally) is different from inherit (receive from a family member).

definition: Having many small parts or details that are closely connected and hard to understand.
examples: The tailor sewed an intricate pattern on the wedding gown.
The plot of the film is so intricate that I had to watch it twice.

pattern.example: They built an intricate network of canals.

cloze.sentence: Banking regulations are ___ and take years to understand.

formDrill.sentence: The pattern was ___ carved into the wooden door.

fix.wrong: The watch has many intricacy inside.
fix.right: The watch has many intricacies inside.
fix.why: Intricacy is countable; use the plural 'intricacies' after 'many'.

distractors: Very simple and easy to repeat.
Large and heavy to carry.
Old and in poor condition.
tip: Intricate describes things that are complex but admired, such as art or machines.

definition: To say firmly that something must happen or is true, and not accept a refusal.
examples: She insisted on paying for dinner.
He insisted that he had sent the payment last week.

pattern.rule: insist + on + -ing / noun; insist that + (should) verb
pattern.example: They insisted on seeing the manager.

cloze.sentence: I ___ that you stay for lunch; I have cooked too much.

formDrill.sentence: His ___ on a refund annoyed the shop owner.

fix.wrong: She insisted to pay the bill.
fix.right: She insisted on paying the bill.
fix.why: Insist takes "on + -ing", not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To agree quickly without any argument.
To ask politely for someone's opinion.
To hope that something will happen.
tip: After insist for a demand, the verb can be bare: "I insist that he apologize."

definition: Clear and easy to understand; also thinking clearly and sensibly.
examples: The manual gives a lucid explanation of how the machine works.
Although he was ill, his grandfather was lucid and remembered everything.

pattern.example: She wrote a lucid summary of the case.

cloze.sentence: His ___ writing makes difficult topics easy to follow.

formDrill.sentence: She explained the new policy ___ so everyone understood.

fix.wrong: The speech was very lucidly.
fix.right: The speech was very lucid.
fix.why: Use the adjective lucid after "was"; lucidly is an adverb.

distractors: Confusing and full of difficult words.
Very bright and shiny.
Fond of telling long stories.
tip: Lucid is positive for explanations; for a person, it means thinking clearly, often after illness.

definition: So small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.
examples: The difference in price between the two phones is negligible.
The damage to the car was negligible.

pattern.rule: negligible + noun; usually before nouns like effect, cost, risk
pattern.example: The cost of the upgrade was negligible.

cloze.sentence: Rainfall this year was ___, so the farmers struggled.

formDrill.sentence: Medical ___ cases are a serious problem in some hospitals.

fix.wrong: The effect was negligent.
fix.right: The effect was negligible.
fix.why: Negligent means careless; negligible means too small to matter.

distractors: Large enough to cause major problems.
Easy to ignore because it is boring.
Impossible to measure or count.
tip: Negligible (very small) is not the same as negligent (careless).

definition: Well known for something bad.
examples: Lagos is notorious for its heavy traffic.
He is a notorious liar, so nobody believed him.

pattern.example: The road is notorious for accidents.

cloze.sentence: The company is ___ for paying its suppliers late.

formDrill.sentence: The exam is ___ difficult, and many students fail it.

fix.wrong: He is notorious because of his kindness.
fix.right: He is famous for his kindness.
fix.why: Notorious is only for bad things; use "famous" for good ones.

distractors: Famous and admired for good deeds.
Unknown to most people.
Strict but fair in dealing with others.
tip: Notorious is negative; famous is neutral or positive.

definition: To like one thing or person better than another.
examples: I prefer tea to coffee in the morning.
She preferred working from home because the commute was long.

pattern.rule: prefer A to B; prefer + to-infinitive / -ing
pattern.example: I prefer walking to driving.

cloze.sentence: I would ___ to pay by card, if that is possible.

formDrill.sentence: Do you have a ___ for window or aisle seats?

fix.wrong: I prefer rice than bread.
fix.right: I prefer rice to bread.
fix.why: Use "prefer A to B", not "than".

distractors: To choose something without thinking.
To hope for something that cannot happen.
To refuse something politely.
tip: Remember the doubled r: preferred, preferring.

definition: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen.
examples: Dark clouds gathered, which was an ominous sign for the match.
There was an ominous silence after the manager read the email.

pattern.example: The ominous noise from the engine worried us.

cloze.sentence: The sudden drop in sales was an ___ sign for the company.

formDrill.sentence: The sky turned ___ dark just before the rain.

fix.wrong: The silence was ominious.
fix.right: The silence was ominous.
fix.why: Spell it ominous, with no extra 'i'.

distractors: Cheerful and full of hope.
Very large and impressive in size.
Hidden and difficult to find.
tip: Ominous comes from "omen", a sign of the future.

definition: A situation or statement that seems impossible or contradictory but may be true.
examples: It is a paradox that the more options we have, the less happy we feel.
The paradox of the job is that you need experience to get experience.

pattern.rule: paradox (sing.), paradoxes (pl.); "it is a paradox that + clause"
pattern.example: It is a paradox that he is rich but never has money.

cloze.sentence: It is a ___ that the busiest people often find time for hobbies.

formDrill.sentence: The cheapest option turned out, ___, to be the most expensive.

fix.wrong: These two paradoxs confuse me.
fix.right: These two paradoxes confuse me.
fix.why: Add -es to words ending in -x to make the plural.

distractors: A simple rule that is easy to follow.
A mistake made on purpose.
A strong disagreement between two parties.
tip: A paradox only seems contradictory; a contradiction is actually inconsistent.

definition: To notice or understand something, or to see it in a particular way.
examples: Many customers perceive the brand as expensive.
I perceived a change in her mood as soon as she walked in.

pattern.example: They perceived the delay as a lack of respect.

cloze.sentence: Some people ___ criticism as an attack, but it can be useful feedback.

formDrill.sentence: Public ___ of the police has improved this year.

fix.wrong: They perceive him like a leader.
fix.right: They perceive him as a leader.
fix.why: Use "perceive ... as", not "like".

distractors: To ignore something on purpose.
To describe something in great detail.
To expect something to happen soon.
tip: Spelling: "i before e, except after c" applies in perceive.

definition: To try very hard to do something that is difficult.
examples: Many families struggle to pay rent when prices rise.
He struggled with math all through secondary school.

pattern.rule: struggle + to + verb / struggle + with + noun
pattern.example: She struggled to understand the accent.

cloze.sentence: Small businesses ___ to compete with large online shops.

formDrill.sentence: She ___ with the new software all week.

fix.wrong: He struggles for understanding the lesson.
fix.right: He struggles to understand the lesson.
fix.why: Use "struggle to + verb", not "for + -ing".

distractors: To win easily without effort.
To leave a place in a hurry.
To argue politely in a meeting.
tip: Struggle is also a noun: "a daily struggle", "a struggle for power".

definition: Extremely important because other things depend on it.
examples: Her speech played a pivotal role in winning the vote.
The meeting was pivotal to the success of the deal.

pattern.rule: pivotal + role / moment; pivotal + to / in + noun
pattern.example: The new road was pivotal to the town's growth.

cloze.sentence: The goalkeeper made a ___ save in the last minute.

formDrill.sentence: She played a ___ role in the merger.

fix.wrong: Her work was pivotal on the success of the project.
fix.right: Her work was pivotal to the success of the project.
fix.why: Use "pivotal to" or "pivotal in", not "on".

distractors: Easy to replace if needed.
Happening again and again.
Connected to a small detail only.
tip: Pivotal is stronger than "important": the result turns on it.

definition: Most common or strongest in number, amount or influence.
examples: English is the predominant language in business here.
Rice is the predominant crop in this region.

pattern.example: The predominant color of the flag is green.

cloze.sentence: Cassava is the ___ food in many rural areas.

formDrill.sentence: The audience was ___ young adults.

fix.wrong: The predominant of our customers are students.
fix.right: The majority of our customers are students.
fix.why: Predominant is an adjective, not a noun meaning "most".

distractors: Very rare and found in only a few places.
Easy to forget quickly.
Used only in formal situations.
tip: Predominantly (adverb) is more common than predominant in everyday writing.

definition: Common or widespread at a particular time or in a particular place.
examples: Malaria is still prevalent in many parts of the country.
Fake news is prevalent on social media.

pattern.example: Mobile banking is prevalent among young people.

cloze.sentence: Online scams are increasingly ___ in the city.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of diabetes has risen in recent years.

fix.wrong: Colds are prevalent at the winter.
fix.right: Colds are prevalent in winter.
fix.why: Use "in winter" with no article.

distractors: Rare and difficult to find.
Strongly disliked by most people.
Happening only once in a lifetime.
tip: Prevalent is used for things (often bad) that are widespread, such as diseases or habits.

definition: To believe something is true without having proof.
examples: I assumed the meeting was canceled because nobody answered.
Don't assume that everyone has a smartphone.

pattern.rule: assume + that-clause / noun; be assumed to + verb
pattern.example: We assumed she would be late.

cloze.sentence: Never ___ the customer knows how the app works.

formDrill.sentence: Their plan is based on a false ___ about demand.

fix.wrong: I assumed to get the job.
fix.right: I assumed (that) I would get the job.
fix.why: Assume takes a that-clause, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: To prove something with strong evidence.
To hope something good will happen.
To ask for permission from someone.
tip: Assume can also mean to take on a role: "assume responsibility".

definition: Able to do something well because of training or practice.
examples: She is proficient in three languages.
The job needs someone proficient at using spreadsheets.

pattern.example: He is proficient in Excel.

cloze.sentence: You must be ___ in English to study at this university.

formDrill.sentence: Applicants must show ___ in written English.

fix.wrong: She is proficient on French.
fix.right: She is proficient in French.
fix.why: Use "proficient in" or "at".

distractors: Just beginning to learn something.
Too proud of your own skills.
Slow but very careful in your work.
tip: Proficient is stronger than "competent" but below "expert".

definition: Expressed clearly in few words.
examples: Please keep your summary succinct; the boss has little time.
Her email was short and succinct.

pattern.example: Be succinct in your answers.

cloze.sentence: Give a ___ description of your role in two sentences.

formDrill.sentence: He explained the plan ___ in under a minute.

fix.wrong: She wrote a succint summary.
fix.right: She wrote a succinct summary.
fix.why: Spell it succinct, with 'cc' in the middle.

distractors: Long and full of unnecessary detail.
Rude and impolite in tone.
Written in complicated language.
tip: Succinct is positive: short but complete, unlike "brief" which can miss details.

definition: Very determined and not giving up easily.
examples: She is a tenacious lawyer who never drops a case.
The team was tenacious and won in the last minute.

pattern.example: He is tenacious in chasing his goals.

cloze.sentence: Her ___ efforts finally got the school the funding it needed.

formDrill.sentence: She held on ___ to her dream of becoming a doctor.

fix.wrong: He is tenacious on his goals.
fix.right: He is tenacious about his goals.
fix.why: Use "tenacious about" or "tenacious in".

distractors: Very easily discouraged by failure.
Careful about spending money.
Kind and patient with children.
tip: Tenacious is positive; for a negative tone, say "stubborn".

definition: To make certain that something happens or is true.
examples: Please ensure that all the doors are locked before you leave.
The new system ensures every payment is recorded.

pattern.example: We must ensure that everyone gets paid on time.

cloze.sentence: Please ___ that your phone is switched off during the exam.

formDrill.sentence: The new rules are ___ that every worker is paid on time.

fix.wrong: I ensure you that it will work.
fix.right: I assure you that it will work.
fix.why: Ensure means make certain; assure means promise someone.

distractors: To promise something to a person.
To pay for protection against loss.
To check something only once.
tip: Ensure (make certain), assure (tell someone confidently), insure (pay for protection).

definition: Seen or found everywhere.
examples: Smartphones are now ubiquitous, even in small villages.
Fast-food chains have become ubiquitous in big cities.

pattern.rule: ubiquitous + noun; be ubiquitous in + place
pattern.example: Mobile money is ubiquitous in Kenya.

cloze.sentence: WhatsApp is ___ among Nigerian small businesses.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ of plastic bags has become a serious problem.

fix.wrong: Phones are ubiquitous at everywhere.
fix.right: Phones are ubiquitous.
fix.why: Ubiquitous already means everywhere, so do not add "at everywhere".

distractors: Very expensive and rare.
Available only at certain times.
New and not widely known.
tip: Ubiquitous is formal; in speech, say "everywhere".

definition: Never having happened or existed before.
examples: The country faced an unprecedented rise in food prices.
Ticket sales reached an unprecedented level this year.

pattern.example: The flood caused unprecedented damage.

cloze.sentence: The pandemic led to ___ changes in how we work.

formDrill.sentence: The judge said there was no ___ for this kind of case.

fix.wrong: It was an unprecedented event in our history before.
fix.right: It was an unprecedented event in our history.
fix.why: Unprecedented already means never before, so drop "before".

distractors: Happening regularly every year.
Planned a long time ahead.
Expected by most experts.
tip: A precedent is an earlier example; unprecedented means there was none.

definition: Refusing to change your mind about something.
examples: She was adamant that she would not sell the land.
He is adamant about not lending money to friends.

pattern.rule: adamant + that-clause / adamant + about + noun or -ing
pattern.example: They were adamant that the plan should go ahead.

cloze.sentence: The manager was ___ that no one would get leave in December.

formDrill.sentence: She ___ refused to apologize.

fix.wrong: He is adamant to leave early.
fix.right: He is adamant about leaving early.
fix.why: Adamant is followed by "about" + -ing or a that-clause, not a to-infinitive.

distractors: Willing to listen and change plans.
Worried about what might go wrong.
Pleased with a result after hard work.
tip: Adamant is stronger than "firm" and often suggests refusing to compromise.

definition: To have earned something good or bad because of what you have done.
examples: You worked hard all year, so you deserve a holiday.
He deserved the promotion more than anyone else.

pattern.example: She deserves to win the award.

cloze.sentence: After such a long week, you ___ a good rest.

formDrill.sentence: The ___ students received a scholarship.

fix.wrong: She deserves getting a raise.
fix.right: She deserves a raise.
fix.why: Deserve takes a noun or a to-infinitive, not -ing, in this meaning.

distractors: To hope strongly to get something.
To ask for something politely.
To deliver something to a person.
tip: Deserve can be used for bad things too: "He deserves to be punished."

definition: Worried that something bad may happen.
examples: I felt apprehensive before my first day at the new job.
The students were apprehensive about the results.

pattern.example: She was apprehensive about flying.

cloze.sentence: He felt ___ as he waited for the doctor's call.

formDrill.sentence: She glanced ___ at the clock as the exam began.

fix.wrong: I am apprehensive of the meeting tomorrow.
fix.right: I am apprehensive about the meeting tomorrow.
fix.why: Use "apprehensive about".

distractors: Completely calm and confident.
Angry at being treated unfairly.
Happy about a surprise.
tip: Apprehensive is milder than "terrified" and slightly formal compared with "nervous".

definition: Decided by chance or personal choice, not by a reason or rule.
examples: The teacher's marking seemed arbitrary and unfair.
The price looks arbitrary; nobody can explain it.

pattern.example: The ban was arbitrary and not based on evidence.

cloze.sentence: The company chose the winners in an ___ way, not by any fair test.

formDrill.sentence: The fine was ___ set without any explanation.

fix.wrong: He chose the winner arbitrary.
fix.right: He chose the winner arbitrarily.
fix.why: Use the adverb arbitrarily to describe how he chose.

distractors: Based on careful testing and evidence.
Decided by a court or judge.
Strict and applied to everyone equally.
tip: Arbitrary often suggests unfairness, because there is no clear reason.

definition: Confident and direct in stating what you want or believe, without being rude.
examples: You need to be more assertive if you want a pay rise.
She gave an assertive reply and refused to be pushed around.

pattern.rule: be assertive + with / about; assertive (positive) vs aggressive (negative)
pattern.example: He was assertive with the client about the deadline.

cloze.sentence: Learn to be ___ so people respect your ideas at work.

formDrill.sentence: She spoke ___ and made her point without raising her voice.

fix.wrong: She spoke assertive in the meeting.
fix.right: She spoke assertively in the meeting.
fix.why: Use the adverb assertively to describe how she spoke.

distractors: Quiet and avoiding any disagreement.
Rude and unwilling to listen.
Eager to please everyone.
tip: Assertive is positive; aggressive is negative.

definition: To deal successfully with a difficult situation.
examples: She copes well with the stress of her job.
How did you cope when the power went off for days?

pattern.example: He is coping with a heavy workload.

cloze.sentence: It was hard to ___ with two jobs and three children.

formDrill.sentence: Reading and music are healthy ___ strategies in hard times.

fix.wrong: I cannot cope this workload.
fix.right: I cannot cope with this workload.
fix.why: Cope needs the preposition "with".

distractors: To pay for something with your own money.
To avoid a problem by leaving.
To copy something exactly.
tip: Use "cope with" for problems, never "cope" followed directly by a noun.

definition: Quick to understand a situation and use it to your advantage.
examples: She is an astute businesswoman who spotted the trend early.
That was an astute move to buy shares before the price rose.

pattern.rule: astute + noun (observer, move, businessperson); astute about + noun
pattern.example: He is astute about money.

cloze.sentence: The ___ investor sold before the market crashed.

formDrill.sentence: She ___ noticed that the figures did not add up.

fix.wrong: He is astute on business.
fix.right: He is astute about business.
fix.why: Use "astute about".

distractors: Slow to react to changes around you.
Generous and kind in dealings with others.
Very strict and unwilling to take risks.
tip: Astute often suggests clever judgment about people or money, not book knowledge.

definition: Kind, generous and wanting to help other people.
examples: The benevolent landlord let the family stay without paying rent for a month.
She set up a benevolent fund for sick workers.

pattern.rule: benevolent + noun (fund, leader, gesture); opposite: malevolent
pattern.example: The benevolent donor paid for the school.

cloze.sentence: The ___ owner gave every worker a bonus at Christmas.

formDrill.sentence: She smiled ___ at the children as they sang.

fix.wrong: She is very benevolence to poor families.
fix.right: She is very benevolent to poor families.
fix.why: Use the adjective benevolent, not the noun benevolence.

distractors: Wanting to harm other people.
Proud and unwilling to listen.
Careful about spending money.
tip: Benevolent is formal and often used for charities, leaders or institutions.

definition: To strengthen or support something and make it more effective.
examples: The company hired extra staff to bolster its customer service team.
A good test result bolstered her confidence.

pattern.example: The new law will bolster consumer rights.

cloze.sentence: The team trained hard to ___ their chances of winning.

formDrill.sentence: The new funds ___ the team's confidence last month.

fix.wrong: The news bolstered up his confidence.
fix.right: The news bolstered his confidence.
fix.why: Bolster is transitive and takes no particle "up".

distractors: To weaken something gradually over time.
To hide something from public view.
To break something into smaller pieces.
tip: Bolster is used for abstract things such as confidence, support, defenses and the economy.

definition: To pause before doing or saying something because you are nervous or not sure.
examples: Please don't hesitate to call me if the invoice looks wrong.
She hesitated at the door, then walked into the interview room.

pattern.example: Don't hesitate to message me after hours.

cloze.sentence: When the bank offered him the loan, he did not ___ for a second.

formDrill.sentence: She gave a ___ smile before answering the question.

fix.wrong: Don't hesitate to asking me for help.
fix.right: Don't hesitate to ask me for help.
fix.why: After hesitate, use to + verb, not -ing.

distractors: To act very quickly without thinking.
To refuse something in an angry way.
To forget what you were about to say.

definition: The quality of being short, especially in speech or writing.
examples: The manager praised the brevity of her weekly report.
In a text message, brevity matters more than perfect grammar.

pattern.example: Brevity is important in a CV.

cloze.sentence: The email was a model of ___: just two clear lines.

formDrill.sentence: Please keep your speech ___ because we are short of time.

fix.wrong: Please be brevity in your emails.
fix.right: Please be brief in your emails.
fix.why: After 'be', use the adjective 'brief', not the noun 'brevity'.

distractors: A feeling of great energy and speed.
Too much detail in a long explanation.
Great skill in speaking to a crowd.
tip: Brevity is the noun for "being brief"; do not confuse it with "breeze" or "bravery".

definition: A person or event that causes an important change or action to happen.
examples: The price increase was the catalyst for our move to a cheaper supplier.
Her speech acted as a catalyst for change in the school.

pattern.example: Social media was a catalyst for the protests.

cloze.sentence: The new boss proved to be a ___ for growth in the sales team.

formDrill.sentence: Social media was one of the main ___ for the protests.

fix.wrong: The strike was a catalyst to the reforms.
fix.right: The strike was a catalyst for the reforms.
fix.why: Use "catalyst for" a change.

distractors: A rule that stops people from taking action.
A person who records events as they happen.
A small mistake that slows a project.

definition: Joined together well so that the parts work or fit as one whole.
examples: We need a cohesive plan, not ten separate ideas.
The team became more cohesive after the training trip.

pattern.example: She wrote a cohesive report.

cloze.sentence: Using the same colors and fonts throughout gives the whole website a ___ look.

formDrill.sentence: Good communication builds team ___.
